review.Summary: The paper introduces Kimi-Dev, an open-source 72B SWE LLM, and challenges the dichotomy between Agentless (workflow-based) and agentic (multi-turn) frameworks for software engineering tasks. The authors argue that Agentless training induces transferable skill priors (localization, code edit, self-reflection) that enable efficient adaptation to SWE-Agent frameworks. The training recipe includes mid-training on ~150B tokens of GitHub PR data, cold-start SFT with reasoning trajectories, RL with verifiable rewards, and test-time self-play. Kimi-Dev achieves 60.4% on SWE-bench Verified, the best among workflow approaches, and after lightweight SFT adaptation on 5k publicly-available trajectories, powers SWE-Agents to 48.6% pass@1, comparable to Claude 3.5 Sonnet. The paper provides extensive ablations showing the contribution of each training stage and demonstrates skill transfer through data-efficiency sweeps, turn-limit analysis, stage annotation, and generalization to SWE-bench-live and SWE-bench Multilingual.
Strengths: Novel and well-motivated central thesis: reframing Agentless and agentic paradigms as complementary stages rather than mutually exclusive, with Agentless training serving as skill priors for agentic adaptation.
Strong empirical results: 60.4% on SWE-bench Verified is state-of-the-art among workflow-based approaches, and the 48.6% agentic performance is competitive with Claude 3.5 Sonnet.

Comprehensive ablation studies: the paper systematically evaluates the contribution of each training stage (mid-training, cold-start SFT, RL) through data-efficiency sweeps, end-to-end RL comparisons, and skill-specific analysis.
Open-source release of model weights and code, supporting reproducibility and community adoption.
Thoughtful analysis of skill transfer, including stage annotation of SWE-Agent trajectories and generalization to SWE-bench-live and SWE-bench Multilingual.
The training recipe details (mid-training data curation, RL with adaptive prompt selection, test-time self-play scoring) are thoroughly described in appendices.
Weaknesses: The 60.4% Agentless result relies on heavy test-time scaling (40 patches × 40 tests = 1600 executions per instance), which may be impractical for real-world deployment and makes comparisons with single-attempt methods somewhat unfair.
The agentic adaptation result (48.6%) is notably lower than the Agentless result (60.4%), raising questions about the practical value of the skill prior transfer for end-to-end agentic settings.

The comparison with Claude 3.5 Sonnet (241022) is dated; newer models (e.g., Claude 3.7/4.0) achieve significantly higher scores (62.3%/72.7%), which somewhat diminishes the significance of the comparison.

The claim that 'Agentless training induces skill priors' is supported primarily through empirical observations rather than a rigorous mechanistic or theoretical analysis of why and how these skills transfer.
The mid-training data curation criteria (e.g., discarding PRs with >3 file modifications, using only .py/.md/.rst files) seem somewhat arbitrary and may limit the diversity of training data.
The 'emergent parallel scaling' observation in Appendix F is interesting but not fully integrated into the main narrative or compared with the primary self-play method.
Questions: What is the total computational cost (GPU-hours, wall-clock time) of the complete training recipe (mid-training, cold-start, RL, and evaluation)? This is critical for assessing practical feasibility and reproducibility.

How does the 40×40 self-play performance compare with pass@40 using ground-truth tests? The gap between self-play and pass@N suggests TestWriter limitations - have you analyzed the specific bottlenecks and failure modes?
Have you explored combining the SWE-Agent SFT adaptation with additional RL for the agentic setting? If so, what were the results? If not, what are the plans for this direction?
What is the variance of the 48.6% pass@1 result across different random seeds or evaluation runs? Is this a single-run measurement?

Can you provide more details on the data decontamination methodology? Specifically, how did you ensure that SWE-bench Verified repositories were excluded from all stages of mid-training, cold-start, and RL?

The paper mentions that the RL prior outperforms the SFT prior in most settings. Can you provide a more detailed analysis of the specific skills (localization, code edit, reflection) that improve after RL, beyond the coarse-grained stage annotation?
How does the model perform on SWE-bench Verified when using the Agentless framework with fewer patches/tests (e.g., 5×5 or 10×10)? This would provide a more practical operating point.
Have you considered evaluating the agentic adaptation with different agent frameworks (e.g., OpenHands) to assess the generality of the skill priors across different agent interfaces?
Limitations: The paper could more explicitly discuss the computational and environmental costs of the training recipe, particularly the 150B-token mid-training and the large-scale RL rollouts.

The potential negative societal impact of automated code generation (e.g., introduction of bugs, security vulnerabilities, or displacement of human developers) is mentioned only briefly in the ethics statement and could be expanded.
The paper acknowledges the coarse-grained nature of the reflection skill analysis but could provide more detail on how the stage annotation was validated for accuracy.
The generalization results on SWE-bench-live and SWE-bench Multilingual are presented in the appendix and could benefit from more thorough discussion in the main text.
The paper does not discuss the potential for the model to be used for malicious purposes (e.g., generating code for exploits) beyond the general agent safety statement.

review.Summary: This paper introduces Kimi-Dev, a 72B open-source SWE LLM that achieves 60.4% on SWE-bench Verified, the best among workflow-based (Agentless) approaches. The core contribution is a novel training recipe that includes mid-training (~150B tokens), cold-start SFT, reinforcement learning with execution-based rewards, and test-time self-play. The paper's central thesis is that Agentless training induces transferable skill priors—such as bug localization, code repair, and self-reflection—that serve as an effective foundation for efficient SWE-Agent adaptation. The authors demonstrate that with only 5k publicly-available trajectories for SFT, Kimi-Dev powers SWE-Agents to 48.6% pass@1, on par with Claude 3.5 Sonnet. Extensive ablations show that each stage of the Agentless training recipe contributes to downstream agentic performance, with the RL-trained model consistently outperforming other priors across various data scales. The paper also shows generalization to SWE-bench-live and SWE-bench Multilingual.
Strengths: Novel conceptual contribution: reframes Agentless and agentic paradigms as complementary rather than mutually exclusive, arguing that structured workflow training induces transferable skill priors
Strong empirical results: achieves state-of-the-art performance (60.4%) among workflow-based approaches on SWE-bench Verified with a 72B open-source model
Comprehensive ablation studies: systematically evaluates the contribution of each training stage (mid-training, SFT, RL) to both Agentless and agentic performance across multiple data scales
Open-sourced model, code, and detailed experimental setup, facilitating reproducibility and further research
Thorough generalization analysis to SWE-bench-live and SWE-bench Multilingual, demonstrating transfer beyond the primary benchmark
Honest discussion of limitations, including TestWriter false positives and the coarse-grained nature of the reflection skill analysis
Weaknesses: The 'skill prior' concept is somewhat qualitative; the paper lacks a rigorous formalization or causal analysis of which specific skills transfer and why
The agentic adaptation result (48.6%) is not state-of-the-art, with several proprietary and open-weight models achieving higher performance under agentic frameworks
The claim that 'self-reflection transfers from long CoT to multi-turn interactions' relies on heuristic stage annotations by an LLM and could be more rigorously validated
The paper is dense and could benefit from clearer organization, particularly in the experimental sections
Limited comparison with alternative training approaches for agentic adaptation, such as starting from other strong base models or using different trajectory data sources
Questions: Could you provide a more rigorous definition or formalization of what constitutes a 'skill prior'? How would one measure the presence or strength of such priors independently of downstream task performance?

The paper shows that the RL prior outperforms other priors in most settings. What specific aspects of the RL training (e.g., execution-based rewards, curriculum learning, positive example reinforcement) contribute most to this advantage?

In Figure 5, the SFT prior shows a significant degradation with 200 trajectories. Could you elaborate on the potential causes and whether this is a consistent phenomenon across different random seeds?
The reflection skill analysis relies on LLM-based stage annotation. What is the agreement rate of this annotation with human judgment? Could you provide some validation of the annotation quality?
How does the performance of Kimi-Dev compare when using different agentic frameworks (e.g., OpenHands) instead of SWE-Agent?
The paper mentions emergent parallel scaling. Could you discuss the computational cost of this approach compared to simple majority voting?
What are the main failure modes of the model in the agentic setting? Could you provide error analysis on instances where the model fails despite having strong skill priors?
Limitations: The paper primarily focuses on SWE-bench Verified, which limits the generalizability of the findings to other software engineering tasks
The agentic adaptation uses trajectories from a single source (SWE-Smith), which may introduce biases from the proprietary model used to collect them
The analysis of skill transfer is largely behavioral and lacks mechanistic understanding of how the training induces these skills
The TestWriter component exhibits false positives during training, which could affect the reliability of the RL rewards
Potential negative societal impact: automated code repair tools could be misused, and the paper's advocacy for agent safety is brief
The paper does not discuss the computational and environmental costs of the extensive training recipe in detail

review.Summary: The paper introduces Kimi-Dev, a 72B open-source SWE LLM trained with a structured 'Agentless' recipe (mid-training on 150B tokens, cold-start SFT with long CoT, RL with execution-based rewards, and test-time self-play), achieving 60.4% on SWE-bench Verified, the best among workflow-based approaches. The central contribution is the reframing of Agentless training not as a final deliverable but as a way to induce 'skill priors' (localization, code edit, self-reflection) that enable efficient and effective adaptation to SWE-Agent frameworks. With only 5k public SWE-Agent trajectories for SFT, Kimi-Dev powers SWE-Agents to 48.6% pass@1, on par with Claude 3.5 Sonnet. The paper provides extensive ablations showing that the RL-trained prior (Kimi-Dev) adapts more efficiently and effectively than mid-trained or SFT-only priors, and that these skills generalize to SWE-bench-live and Multilingual benchmarks.
Strengths: Novel and well-motivated central thesis: reframing Agentless training as skill priors for agentic training, challenging the common dichotomy.
State-of-the-art results on SWE-bench Verified among workflow-based approaches (60.4%) with an open-weight 72B model.
Comprehensive experimental validation: ablations on each training stage, data-efficiency sweeps with multiple priors, and end-to-end SWE-Agent RL comparison.
Strong evidence for the skill-prior hypothesis: the RL prior consistently outperforms other priors in nearly all adaptation settings, with significant data efficiency gains.
Analysis of skill transfer (BugFixer and reflection) provides interpretable evidence of how Agentless training benefits agentic behavior.
Open-source release of model weights and code, enhancing reproducibility and community impact.
Weaknesses: Full training recipe is not fully reproducible: mid-training data (150B tokens) and cold-start data (R1-generated) are not released, limiting replication of the complete pipeline.
The agentic evaluation is primarily based on SFT adaptation (48.6%); the end-to-end SWE-Agent RL results are presented only for minimal cold-start settings and on a subset, not for the full model.
The reflection skill analysis is acknowledged as coarse-grained, conflating reflection with other behaviors like test-writing.
Potential distributional bias from SWE-smith trajectories (collected with Claude 3.7) is not deeply discussed, though the minimal-SFT RL comparison partially mitigates this.

Generalization results (SWE-bench-live, Multilingual) are relegated to the appendix and show diminishing advantage of the RL prior with more SFT data, which could temper the claims of transferability.
Questions: Could you release the mid-training data or a representative subset to enable full reproducibility of the training recipe?
Why is the end-to-end SWE-Agent RL result for the final Kimi-Dev model (with full 5k SFT trajectories) not reported on SWE-bench Verified? The current 48.6% agentic result is from SFT only.
How do you ensure that the SWE-smith trajectories do not introduce distributional bias that might favor certain problem types, and how does this affect the generalization claims?
Can you provide a more fine-grained analysis of the reflection skill, perhaps by isolating the TestWriter's contribution in the Stage-3 to final performance gain?
Would the skill-prior hypothesis hold if a different base model (e.g., Qwen3-Coder or a larger model) were used? Have you tested the recipe on other base models beyond Qwen2.5-72B-Base?
In Figure 7, the end-to-end RL results show only marginal gains of the RL prior over the SFT prior. Could you comment on the statistical significance and stability of these differences across runs?
Limitations: The paper does not release the mid-training data or the R1-generated cold-start data, limiting full reproducibility of the training pipeline.
The agentic evaluation is mostly based on SFT adaptation, and the end-to-end agentic RL is not evaluated on the full SWE-bench Verified set with the final model.
The reflection skill analysis is acknowledged as coarse-grained and may overestimate the contribution of reflection by including other agentic behaviors.
The generalization experiments on SWE-bench-live and Multilingual are only presented in the appendix and show mixed results, with the advantage of the RL prior diminishing when more SFT data is used.
Potential societal impact is briefly mentioned, but the paper could more thoroughly discuss the risks of automated code generation and the importance of robust evaluation in real-world deployments.

The paper is strong in several dimensions:
- **Originality**: The core idea of reframing Agentless training as skill priors for agentic training is novel and well-motivated. The paper challenges a common dichotomy in the field.
- **Quality**: The experimental methodology is thorough. The authors conduct ablations on each training stage, sweep SFT data amounts, compare multiple priors (Base, MT, SFT, RL), and even run end-to-end SWE-Agent RL on top of the priors. The results are compelling and support the central claims.
- **Clarity**: The paper is well-structured and clearly written. The appendices provide extensive details on data curation, prompts, and case studies.
- **Significance**: The results are state-of-the-art for open-weight models under 100B params in the Agentless setting, and competitive in the agentic setting. The insight that structured skill priors can scaffold agentic training is likely to influence future work on training coding agents.

The training recipe includes mid-training on ~150B tokens of GitHub PR data, cold-start SFT with reasoning trajectories, RL with verifiable rewards, and test-time self-play. Kimi-Dev achieves 60.4% on SWE-bench Verified, the best among workflow-based approaches, and after lightweight SFT adaptation on 5k publicly available trajectories, powers SWE-Agents to 48.6% pass@1, comparable to Claude 3.5 Sonnet. Extensive ablations demonstrate the contribution of each training stage, and generalization is shown on SWE-bench-live and SWE-bench Multilingual. The model, code, and experimental details are open-sourced.
Strengths: Novel and well-motivated central thesis: reframing Agentless training as inducing transferable skill priors for agentic adaptation, rather than treating the two paradigms as mutually exclusive.
Strong empirical results: 60.4% on SWE-bench Verified is state-of-the-art among workflow-based approaches with an open-weight 72B model.
Comprehensive ablation studies systematically evaluating the contribution of mid-training, cold-start SFT, and RL to both Agentless and agentic performance across multiple data scales.
Thorough analysis of skill transfer, including data-efficiency sweeps, turn-limit analysis, stage-level skill characterization, and end-to-end RL comparison.
Generalization studies to SWE-bench-live and SWE-bench Multilingual provide evidence of transfer beyond the primary benchmark.
Open-source release of model weights, code, and detailed experimental setup, supporting reproducibility and community adoption.
Honest discussion of limitations, including TestWriter false positives and the coarse-grained nature of reflection skill analysis.
Weaknesses: The 'skill prior' concept is largely qualitative; the paper provides behavioral evidence but lacks a rigorous formalization or mechanistic analysis of what specific skills transfer and why.
The agentic adaptation result (48.6%) is not state-of-the-art, with several newer proprietary models (e.g., Claude 3.7/4.0) achieving higher scores; the comparison with Claude 3.5 Sonnet is dated.
The full training recipe is not fully reproducible: the mid-training data (150B tokens) and cold-start data (R1-generated) are not released, limiting replication of the complete pipeline.
The end-to-end SWE-Agent RL results are only presented for minimal cold-start settings and on a subset, not for the final model with full SFT adaptation.
The test-time self-play is computationally expensive (40x40 patch-test pairs per instance), which may limit practical adoption and makes comparisons with single-attempt methods somewhat unfair.
The reflection skill analysis relies on LLM-based stage annotation, which is acknowledged as coarse-grained and may conflate reflection with other behaviors like test-writing.
The computational cost (GPU-hours, wall-clock time) of the full training recipe is not quantified, which is a significant omission given the scale of the approach.
Questions: What is the total computational cost (GPU-hours, wall-clock time) of the complete training recipe, including mid-training, cold-start SFT, RL, and evaluation?

Can you provide a more rigorous definition or formalization of what constitutes a 'skill prior'? How would one measure the presence or strength of such priors independently of downstream task performance?
Why is the end-to-end SWE-Agent RL result for the final Kimi-Dev model (with full 5k SFT trajectories) not reported on SWE-bench Verified? The current 48.6% agentic result is from SFT only.
How does the 40x40 self-play performance compare with pass@40 using ground-truth tests? What are the specific bottlenecks and failure modes of the TestWriter?
Have you explored combining the SWE-Agent SFT adaptation with additional RL for the agentic setting? If so, what were the results?
How does the performance of Kimi-Dev compare when using different agentic frameworks (e.g., OpenHands) instead of SWE-Agent?
Can you provide validation of the LLM-based stage annotation for the reflection skill analysis, e.g., agreement rate with human judgment?
How sensitive are the results to the choice of the base model (Qwen2.5-72B)? Have you tested the recipe on other base models?
What is the variance of the 48.6% pass@1 result across different random seeds or evaluation runs? Is this a single-run measurement?
Can you provide more details on the data decontamination methodology to ensure SWE-bench Verified repositories were excluded from all training stages?
Limitations: The paper does not release the mid-training data or the R1-generated cold-start data, limiting full reproducibility of the training pipeline.
The agentic evaluation is mostly based on SFT adaptation; end-to-end agentic RL is not evaluated on the full SWE-bench Verified set with the final model.
The reflection skill analysis is coarse-grained and may overestimate the contribution of reflection by conflating it with other agentic behaviors.
Evaluation is primarily confined to the SWE-bench family; results on broader coding benchmarks (e.g., HumanEval, MBPP) or other agentic tasks would strengthen generalizability claims.
The computational and environmental costs of the extensive training recipe are not discussed in detail, which may limit practical feasibility for many research groups.
The potential negative societal impact of automated code generation (e.g., introduction of bugs, security vulnerabilities, or displacement of human developers) is mentioned only briefly.
The SWE-Smith trajectories used for agentic SFT are collected from proprietary models, and the potential distribution shift and its implications are not deeply discussed.
